one_line_contribution: An intervention-based blame taxonomy for memory-induced failures in a multi-step agent: on ALFWorld games that the agent solves at k=0 but fails at k=3, re-run every single-item and pairwise removal to ask whether the harm belongs to one retrieved item, to a pair, or to the set, and test whether a culprit's harm survives re-embedding in a different background set.
closest_prior_work: Two verified threats. (1) arXiv:2608.11888 'Agent Skills Can Be Harmful: An Empirical Study of Skill-Induced Failures in LLM Agents' (2026-08-12, verified by `paper` on S2, 1 citation): its stated method is 'a differential analysis framework that attributes a failure or regression to a skill by comparing a target skill-guided run against a no-skill or semantically matched skill reference run that solves the same task', plus a taxonomy-guided attribution tool. Retrieved ALFWorld expert trajectories are procedural skills - the proposal's own brief measures that a 3-exemplar static procedure prompt recovers +12.4 of the k=3 gain - so this is the same primitive (differential with/without on the same task, with a matched reference) applied to the same object class, with a failure taxonomy already attached. It directly refutes the abstract's headline claim of 'the first item-level blame ground truth for naturally accumulated agent memory'. What it does not appear to do is the item-vs-set contrast (pairwise removal, re-embedding in a second background set), which is the part of this proposal that survives. (2) arXiv:2604.05467 CUE-R (verified on S2): 'a lightweight intervention-based framework for measuring per-evidence-item operational utility in single-shot RAG' with REMOVE/REPLACE/DUPLICATE and 'an operational evidence-role taxonomy for interpreting intervention outcomes' - i.e. the exact intervention protocol and the exact taxonomy idea, one setting away (single-shot RAG rather than multi-step). Also close on setting: arXiv:2608.20627 AgenticRAG-FP (verified on S2), an interventional benchmark that injects a certified fault, re-executes the downstream trajectory and scores diagnosers against known ground truth; it blames hops rather than items and uses injected rather than natural faults. arXiv:2607.22520 'The Regression Tax: Decomposing Why Skills Help and Hurt LLM Agents' (HF) already decomposes procedural-item regressions into context effects, misinterpretation and suppressed verification - a competing causal account the proposal never contrasts. MemAudit arXiv:2605.23723 verified on S2 (the proposal reports its `paper` lookup failed; it resolves now, 4 citations) and is correctly positioned as poisoning-specific.
strongest_objection: The headline number P1 is biased upward by its own estimator, and the plan contains no null for the statistic it actually computes. Single-culprit is declared if the MAXIMUM over three 4-seed removal cells clears p0-0.25, with no multiplicity correction and no comparison to the no-op cell. With n=4 seeds the estimate lives on a 5-point grid: if harm were genuinely diffuse and every removal left true p(S-i)=0.4, each cell reads >=0.5 with probability P(X>=2 of 4 at 0.4)=0.53, so the max over three cells clears the bar about 89% of the time. A diffuse world therefore reports a single-culprit majority, and P1 >= 0.6 is close to unfalsifiable in practice even though the entailment check calls the falsifier reachable in principle. Two further mechanisms push the same way and are uncontrolled: harmed games are selected on p3 <= 0.25 from the same seeds used in the comparison, so any fresh re-run regresses upward (the plan runs a no-op repeat that would fix this, then does not use it in the taxonomy rule, comparing to the selection-time p0 instead); and every S-i cell is a k=2 prompt while every reference cell is k=3, so 'removal restores success' is confounded with 'a shorter context helps on this game' - a set-size effect the brief's own k-sweep says is real (k=1 -> k=3 is worth ~+7 net). Because P1's taxonomy defines the population for P2, P3, P4, P5 and P7 (the entailment check lists exactly this dependency), one lenient rule inflates the entire result table at once. On top of that, 3 of 7 predictions cannot do work as written: P4 is entailed (the static arm is scored by an absolute p >= 0.75 on games selected for p0 >= 0.75, with no paired fresh k=0), P2's odds ratio has a CI containing its own falsifier at the expected 30-60 single-culprit items, and P6's falsifier is a conjunction whose +/-2-point equivalence band sits inside a +/-3.5-point CI.
what_would_fix_it: 1) Make the null match the statistic: run three no-op repeats per harmed game, not one, compute the same max-over-three restoration rule on them, and report the single-culprit fraction as the excess over that empirical null with a permutation CI; report P1 as an excess, not a raw count. 2) Hold set size fixed: for each i, run S with item i replaced by a token- and type-matched neutral filler alongside S-i, so 'this item is harmful' is separated from 'k=2 beats k=3 here'. The round's own binding rule already asks for token-matched replacement and the proposal uses it only for the planted control. 3) Score restoration against the fresh no-op cell rather than the selection-time p0, which removes the winner's-curse regression the p3 <= 0.25 filter creates. 4) Rescore P4 as a paired static-minus-fresh-k0 difference on the same new seeds. 5) Either pre-register the culprit count P2's odds ratio needs (the entailment check estimates ~150 single-culprit games) or collapse to a two-class contrast with a stated MDE, and split P6 into a rate-ratio CI plus a separately powered diffuse-share claim. 6) Reframe the contribution honestly against arXiv:2608.11888 and arXiv:2607.22520: the new thing is item-vs-set causation and blame transfer across background sets, not the first item-level blame ground truth, and the abstract must say so.
missing_baseline: A set-size- and token-matched replacement cell (S with item i swapped for a matched neutral filler) as the counterfactual for each removal, plus a matched no-op null computed with the same max-over-three rule; secondarily, a random-item-removal calibration on unharmed/helped games to measure how often a removal appears to 'restore' success where there is nothing to restore. Without these, every restoration count is confounded with context length and with regression from the p3 <= 0.25 selection.
